When atoms of these gases are excited by the flow of electrons in the discharge tubes, they emit photons of visible light in their characteristic spectral colors. All noble gases have the maximum number of electrons possible in t](/images/section_10/ca5fe25e5cb9f31033ecccc811fbebd4.jpg)

**The noble gases.** Helium, neon, argon, krypton, and xenon, all monatomic elements, are five of the six known noble gases. When atoms of these gases are excited by the flow of electrons in the discharge tubes, they emit photons of visible light in their characteristic spectral colors. All noble gases have the maximum number of electrons possible in their outer shell (2 for helium, 8 for all others), so they do not form chemical compounds easily.

entries.notes: Find a matched photograph of identical chemiluminescent sticks in hot versus ice water, with explicit temperature-condition labels. Brightness depends on exposure as well as reaction rate; avoid fabricated quantitative brightness comparisons.
entries.original_markdown:
![Figure 14.2 The Effect of Temperature on Reaction Rates](/images/section_18/ab6a96bbd04d93a7b0d6aa1111147e20.jpg)

At high temperature, the reaction that produces light in a chemiluminescent light stick occurs more rapidly, producing more photons of light per unit time. Consequently, the light glows brighter in hot water (left) than in ice water (right).

![Figure 23.4 Aqueous Solutions of Vanadium Ions in Oxidation States of +2 to +5](/images/section_27/c21e25a2d4be77abc47e545ccf92446c.jpg)

Because vanadium ions with different oxidation states have different numbers of *d* electrons, aqueous solutions of the ions have different colors: in acid V(V) forms the pale yellow \[VO<sub>2</sub>\]<sup>+</sup> ion; V(IV) is the blue vanadyl ion \[VO\]<sup>2+</sup>; and V(III) and V(II) exist as the hydrated V<sup>3+</sup> (blue-green) and V<sup>2+</sup> (violet) ions, respectively.

![Figure 23.5 Compounds of Manganese in Oxidation States +2 to +7](/images/section_27/355ce2892281bd83ab0834a68552d267.jpg)

Like vanadium, compounds of manganese in different oxidation states have different numbers of *d* electrons, which leads to compounds with different colors: the Mn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) ion is pale pink; Mn(OH)<sub>3</sub>, which contains Mn(III), is a dark brown solid; MnO<sub>2</sub>, which contains Mn(IV), is a black solid; and aqueous solutions of Mn(VI) and Mn(VII) contain the green manganate ion \[MnO<sub>4</sub>\]<sup>2−</sup> and the purple permanganate ion \[MnO<sub>4</sub>\]<sup>−</sup>, respectively.
